citation: Fanning J, Roberts S, Hillman CH, Mullen SP, Ritterband L, McAuley E. (2017). A smartphone “app”-delivered randomized factorial trial targeting physical activity in adults. Journal of Behavioral Medicine, 40(5), 712–729.
adherence_problem: Insufficient physical activity; adoption/maintenance challenge [study rationale]
intervention: Smartphone self-monitoring app with tracking, feedback, and education; factorial add-on modules for goal setting and points-based feedback
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; feedback; education; goal setting; points-based feedback/reinforcement
result_and_DOI: All groups increased MVPA by >11 min/day; points-based feedback was associated with higher MVPA and more favorable psychosocial/app-usage outcomes; goal-setting access was associated with higher app usage. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10865-017-9838-y

citation: Carr LJ, Dunsiger SI, Lewis B, Ciccolo JT, Hartman S, Bock B, Dominick G, Marcus BH. (2013). Randomized controlled trial testing an internet physical activity intervention for sedentary adults. Health Psychology, 32(3), 328–336.
population: Sedentary adults; N=53; enhanced Internet n=25, standard Internet n=28; mean age approximately 37 years
adherence_problem: Sedentary behavior / insufficient physical activity; adoption and maintenance over 6 months [study rationale]
intervention: Enhanced Step into Motion website with tailored motivational messages, PA tracking/logging calendar, pedometer-supported self-monitoring, goal setting, progress feedback, discussion forum/social support, exercise videos, geographic mapping, peer PA updates, and reminder emails
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; goal setting; feedback on progress; tailored motivational feedback; social support; observational learning/modeling; environmental support; prompts
outcome: Self-reported physical activity (7-day Physical Activity Recall; minutes/week); proportion meeting 150 min/week guideline
result_and_DOI: Enhanced Internet produced a greater increase in PA than standard Internet at 3 months (p=.03), but the between-group difference was not maintained at 6 months (p=.44). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028962

citation: Zhou M, Fukuoka Y, Mintz Y, Goldberg K, Kaminsky P, Flowers E, Aswani A. (2018). Evaluating Machine Learning–Based Automated Personalized Daily Step Goals Delivered Through a Mobile Phone App: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 6(1), e28.
population: Adult university staff employees; N=64; mean age 41.1 ± 11.3 years; 83% female
adherence_problem: Fixed nonpersonalized step goals may discourage continued physical activity [study rationale]
intervention: CalFit smartphone app with real-time step monitoring and push notifications; intervention received automated personalized adaptive daily step goals generated from prior step/goal data; active control received fixed 10,000-step goals
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; personalized/adaptive goal setting; prompts/notifications; goal-attainment feedback
outcome: Objectively measured daily step count; step-goal attainment; secondary self-report measures
result_and_DOI: From run-in to 10 weeks, mean steps decreased in both groups, but the decrease was smaller with personalized adaptive goals (−390 vs −1350 steps/day); net between-group difference 960 steps/day (95% CI 90–1830; p=.03). DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/mhealth.9117

citation: Slootmaker SM, Chinapaw MJM, Schuit AJ, Seidell JC, van Mechelen W. (2009). Feasibility and Effectiveness of Online Physical Activity Advice Based on a Personal Activity Monitor: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 11(3), e27.
population: Dutch office workers; N=102 randomized; age 23–39 years; mean age 31.8 ± 3.5 years
target_behavior: Sedentary, light, moderate, vigorous, and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (minutes/week)
adherence_problem: Low physical activity and poor awareness of insufficient activity [study rationale]
intervention: Personal Activity Monitor (PAM) plus PAM COACH website with uploaded activity scores, personal goal setting, activity logs/graphs, individualized activity advice based on goals/preferences/barriers, motivational feedback, peer comparison, and self-monitoring
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; feedback; goal setting; tailored advice; action planning through preferred activities; barrier-focused problem solving; social comparison
duration: 3 months; follow-up at 8 months (5 months post-intervention)
outcome: Self-reported sedentary, light, moderate, vigorous, and MVPA minutes/week; PA determinants; fitness; body composition; program use
result_and_DOI: No significant intervention effect on PA outcomes after 3 months or at 8-month follow-up; usage was moderate and tailored advice was often rated unappealing. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.1139

citation: Hurling R, Catt M, De Boni M, Fairley BW, Hurst T, Murray P, Richardson A, Sodhi JS. (2007). Using Internet and Mobile Phone Technology to Deliver an Automated Physical Activity Program: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 9(2), e7.
population: Healthy adults; N=77; mean age 40.4 ± 7.6 years; mean BMI 26.3 ± 3.4 kg/m²
target_behavior: Moderate physical activity; leisure-time physical activity
adherence_problem: Insufficient physical activity; barriers to initiating and maintaining planned exercise [study rationale]
intervention: 9-week automated Internet and mobile phone program with wrist-worn accelerometer; real-time web feedback, tailored barrier solutions, weekly exercise scheduling, mobile/email reminders, message board/social interaction, and activity feedback; control received accelerometer monitoring without program support
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; real-time feedback; tailored barrier problem solving; action/exercise planning; prompts/reminders; social support; perceived-control/intention support
outcome: Accelerometer-measured moderate physical activity; self-reported leisure-time physical activity; perceived control; exercise intention/expectation
result_and_DOI: Intervention participants had higher moderate physical activity than controls by accelerometer (p=.02) and leisure-time self-report (p=.03); the reported accelerometer-measured between-group increase was 2 h 18 min/week. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.9.2.e7

citation: Wang JB, Cadmus-Bertram LA, Natarajan L, White MM, Madanat H, Nichols JF, Ayala GX, Pierce JP. (2015). Wearable Sensor/Device (Fitbit One) and SMS Text-Messaging Prompts to Increase Physical Activity in Overweight and Obese Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Telemedicine and e-Health, 21(10), 782–792.
population: Overweight or obese adults below recommended PA levels; N=67; mean age 48.2 ± 11.7 years; 91% female
target_behavior: Daily steps; moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA); total physical activity
adherence_problem: Insufficient physical activity; maintaining engagement beyond an initial response [study rationale]
intervention: All participants used Fitbit One for self-monitoring with instant tracker feedback plus web/mobile-app summaries; intervention group additionally received three SMS physical-activity prompts per day for 6 weeks
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; immediate performance feedback; summary feedback; prompts/cues via SMS
outcome: Actigraph-measured steps, MVPA, and total PA at baseline and week 6; Fitbit-measured weekly steps and active minutes
result_and_DOI: No between-group difference in primary PA outcomes at 6 weeks. SMS produced a short-lived week-1 advantage (+1,266 steps and higher active minutes), but this effect did not persist; Fitbit-only participants showed a small within-group MVPA increase at week 6. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1089/tmj.2014.0176

citation: Gell NM, Wadsworth DD. (2015). The Use of Text Messaging to Promote Physical Activity in Working Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Physical Activity and Health, 12(6), 756–763.
population: Full-time working women; N=87; intervention n=41, control n=46; mean age approximately mid-to-late 40s
adherence_problem: Maintaining physical activity despite work, time, weather, and other common barriers [study rationale]
intervention: Approximately three targeted SMS messages per week for 24 weeks; messages were motivational, informational, and activity-specific, including guideline information, activity suggestions, goal setting, relapse prevention, social support, self-monitoring, time management, reinforcement, and barrier strategies; both groups received walking maps and website resources
BCT_or_mechanism: Prompts/cues; goal setting; relapse prevention; social support; self-monitoring; time management; reinforcement; barrier problem solving; informational/motivational support
outcome: Pedometer steps/day; exercise self-efficacy at baseline, 12 weeks, and 24 weeks
result_and_DOI: Intervention group had higher steps/day than control at 12 weeks (6540 vs 5685; p=.01), but not significantly at 24 weeks (6867.7 vs 6189.0; p=.06). Steps did not increase from baseline; the mid-intervention difference reflected a larger decline in controls, consistent with maintenance rather than absolute increase. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1123/jpah.2013-0144

citation: Maddison R, Pfaeffli L, Whittaker R, Stewart R, Kerr A, Jiang Y, Kira G, Leung W, Dalleck L, Carter K, Rawstorn J. (2015). A mobile phone intervention increases physical activity in people with cardiovascular disease: Results from the HEART randomized controlled trial. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 22(6), 701–709.
population: Adults with clinically stable ischaemic heart disease; N=171; intervention n=85, usual care n=86; age ≥18 years
target_behavior: Leisure-time physical activity; walking; prescribed aerobic exercise
adherence_problem: Low participation/adherence in exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation due to psychological, physical, and access barriers [study rationale]
intervention: 24-week personalized automated mHealth cardiac-rehabilitation program: SMS exercise prescriptions and behavior-change messages plus secure website with video messages, progress tracking, goal setting, barrier identification/solutions, exercise tips, role models, and personalized feedback; intervention participants also received a pedometer; control received usual cardiac-rehabilitation care
BCT_or_mechanism: Personalized exercise prescription; goal setting; self-monitoring; feedback on progress; action scheduling; barrier problem solving; prompts/messages; role modeling; social support; self-efficacy support
outcome: Peak VO2; self-reported leisure-time physical activity and walking; self-efficacy; quality of life
result_and_DOI: No between-group improvement in peak VO2 at 24 weeks, but leisure-time PA favored intervention by 110.2 min/week (p=.05) and walking by 151.4 min/week (p=.02); self-efficacy to be active also improved. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1177/2047487314535076

citation: Harries T, Eslambolchilar P, Rettie R, Stride C, Walton S, van Woerden HC. (2016). Effectiveness of a smartphone app in increasing physical activity amongst male adults: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Public Health, 16, 925.
population: Healthy male adults; N=165 randomized; age 18–40 years; 152 included in analysis
adherence_problem: Low motivation or awareness to increase everyday walking [study rationale]
intervention: Always-on smartphone app that continuously recorded steps; randomized to no feedback, personal step-count feedback, or personal plus social-comparison feedback against the group average; feedback included current/day/history displays and refreshed every 15 minutes
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; feedback on behavior; historical progress feedback; social comparison (social-feedback arm)
result_and_DOI: Both feedback arms had higher model-estimated step counts than no-feedback control (individual feedback +60%; social feedback +69%); social feedback was not significantly better than individual feedback, and the feedback effect did not significantly change over the 6-week trial. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-016-3593-9

citation: Fukuoka Y, Haskell W, Lin F, Vittinghoff E. (2019). Short- and Long-term Effects of a Mobile Phone App in Conjunction With Brief In-Person Counseling on Physical Activity Among Physically Inactive Women: The mPED Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open, 2(5), e194281.
population: Community-dwelling physically inactive women; N=210; age 25–65 years; mean age 52.4 ± 11.0 years
adherence_problem: Insufficient physical activity plus maintenance of gains after an initial behavior-change phase [study rationale]
intervention: 3-month mPED program combining brief in-person counseling, mobile app, and accelerometer: individualized short- and long-term goals, education, barrier strategies, social support, relapse prevention, daily messages/video, activity diary, automated reminders, and weekly goals increased by 20%; during 6-month maintenance, the plus group continued app + accelerometer while the regular group continued accelerometer only
BCT_or_mechanism: Goal setting; self-monitoring; feedback; graded goals; barrier problem solving; social support; relapse prevention; prompts/reminders; education
result_and_DOI: During the first 3 months, the combined intervention groups increased activity versus control by 2,060 steps/day and 18.2 min/day MVPA. During the next 6 months, continuing the app did not provide a significant maintenance advantage over accelerometer-only maintenance. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2019.4281
